title: Like a trumpeter
hook: the four immeasurables sounded in every direction, like a strong trumpeter

segments.voice: Yesterday: brahmins describing a god none of them had seen, and your line, can you see for yourself. Did you test one idea you inherited? Today the same discourse turns around and offers a way forward. Day five hundred forty-two.

The Pali word behind today's trumpeter is sankhadhama: a conch-blower. Long before loudspeakers, a strong player could lift a conch shell and send one clear note out over the fields. He doesn't aim it. He doesn't send it down one road. The sound simply goes out, and nobody within reach is left out of hearing it. That is the picture the Buddha reaches for near the end of the Tevijja Sutta, the thirteenth of the Long Discourses. Yesterday he took apart a claim. Today he hands the young brahmin Vasettha something to do instead. Today: like a trumpeter.
screen: `A CONCH-BLOWER'S NOTE.` → `IT GOES EVERYWHERE AT ONCE.` → `THE END OF DN 13.`

segments.voice: Vasettha and his friend wanted to know the straight road to union with Brahma, the high god of their teachers. The Buddha has just shown that their teachers never saw Brahma. But he doesn't stop there and walk away. He asks: is Brahma, as you describe him, full of hate or free of it? Free of it, they say. Burdened with possessions or free of them? Free. Then he describes a monk who becomes like that. First, the monk lets go of the five hindrances, and gladness rises. Then he lets a mind of loving-kindness fill one direction, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, around, everywhere, a mind wide, grown great, without measure, free of hate. Then the same with compassion. Then with gladness at others' joy. Then with equanimity. Elsewhere the texts call these four the brahmaviharas, the dwellings of Brahma; they're also called the four immeasurables. And here's the image. As a strong trumpeter makes himself heard in all four directions without any strain, so this mind leaves out no living thing. It doesn't choose who gets to hear. Here is the move. The Buddha takes the brahmins' own goal, union with Brahma, and gives it content. Not a place you travel to by argument, but a heart you grow, one direction at a time. In a number of Buddhist communities the four are still practiced this way, radiating outward, direction by direction. And the image carries one more detail: the conch-blower is heard with little difficulty. The note isn't forced.
screen: `WHAT IS BRAHMA LIKE? FREE OF HATE.` · `ONE DIRECTION, THEN THE NEXT.` · `FOUR IMMEASURABLES.` · `HEARD EVERYWHERE, WITHOUT STRAIN.` · then, large: `LIKE A TRUMPETER.`

segments.voice: Pick one of the four: kindness, compassion, gladness for others, or calm. Just one. Sit, and let it face forward, toward whoever is in front of you, near or far. Then let it turn to your right. Behind you. To your left. Then above and below. You don't need to picture anyone. Just let the wish go out the way a note goes out, without pushing. If it goes thin, come back to the breath and send it again. The bell holds the time.
brahmavihara. The four immeasurables from the Tevijja Sutta: a mind of goodwill heard in every direction, leaving no one out, without strain. Today's word.
Your line: the note isn't forced. Today, when you walk into a room, let one quiet note of goodwill go out to everyone in it, not just the people you like. Day five hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: In many Buddhist traditions people practice the four brahmaviharas by sending loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity outward in each direction in turn, often as part of a daily sit or a chanted metta practice.

myth: after showing the brahmins' teachers never saw Brahma, the Buddha simply leaves
he goes on to teach a way to become like Brahma: the four immeasurables.
in DN 13 the mind of loving-kindness is spread one direction after another, then everywhere
first one quarter, then the second, third and fourth, then above, below and all around.

the point is ease: he is heard in all four directions without difficulty.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. you've just shown two young brahmins that their teachers never saw the god they describe. they still want union with Brahma. what do you do?
options: tell them to drop the goal entirely.
ask what Brahma is like, then teach a heart that becomes like that.
send them back to their teachers.
fork.reveal: he asks whether Brahma is free of hate, then teaches the four immeasurables as the way to become like Brahma.

original.note: Pali brahmavihara: a dwelling of Brahma. the name for the four immeasurables.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving-kindness is a warm feeling toward people you already like.
what it means: in DN 13 it is spread to every direction, without measure, leaving no one out, like a trumpet's note.
what a scholar hears: the Tevijja Sutta gives the brahmavihara formula as the Buddha's answer to the brahmins' goal of union with Brahma (brahma-sahavyata).

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 13 (Tevijja Sutta), the four brahmaviharas and the trumpeter simile

notes: DN 13 paraphrased. Rhys Davids translated it in Dialogues of the Buddha I (1899), including the trumpeter simile, but the exact wording was not quoted because it could not be confirmed word for word.
Confirm the questioning sequence (is Brahma with or without possessions, with or without hate) and that the hindrances are abandoned before the brahmaviharas in this sutta.
The opening scene uses a conch or horn as the picture; the Pali is sankhadhama (conch-blower). Confirm the framing.

Reviewer: the word 'brahmavihara' may not appear in DN 13 itself (it names the practice as the way to companionship with Brahma); the teach now says 'elsewhere the texts call these four the brahmaviharas'. 'Exactly this order' softened to 'often in this same order'.
Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens with Picture and now names the conch-blower (sankhadhama); cut the unsourced Many Buddhists claim and the horn-player filler line.
